paper_information.title: Maize Diseases and Their Sustainable Management in India: Current Status and Future Perspectives
paper_information.journal_or_source: Innovative Approaches in Diagnosis and Management of Crop Diseases, Vol 2
paper_information.abstract_summary: Information embodied in this review pertains to the common diseases affecting maize production in India. The major diseases in the country are three downy mildews, four foliar, leaf, and sheath blight and two pre-flowering, three post-flowering stalk rots. Loss estimates in India have been put at around 13.2%, but actual losses can be as high as 80% in natural and artificial created epiphytotic conditions.
paper_information.research_objective: To assess the present status of diseases and researchable area to alleviate losses which would further necessitate the development of bio-rational and climate-resilient integrated disease management (IDM) schedule.
important_findings: Maize in India is affected by about 35 diseases predominantly of fungal and bacterial origin.
Estimated annual yield loss in India is 13.2%, but actual losses can reach up to 80% under epiphytotic conditions.
Turcicum leaf blight, maydis leaf blight, post-flowering stalk rots, ear and cob rot, and banded leaf and sheath blight are prevalent throughout the country.

general: Severe defoliation especially during the grain-filling period
Starts as long, elliptical, gray-green lesions measuring 3-15 cm in length
early_symptoms: Infection occurs from the lower lamina, gradually extending to the upsides
advanced_symptoms: Lesions mature to tan color with targeted, darkish zones of fungal sporulation
Lesions may coalesce forming enormous blighted areas, and entire leaves may emerge as blighted
visual_field_symptoms: Extensive defoliation during the grain filling period

field_identification: Long, elliptical, gray-green to tan lesions with darkish zones of fungal sporulation

causes_and_risk_factors: High humidity coupled with low temperature and cloudy weather
disease_development_and_spread: Infection occurs from seedling to harvesting, with maximum severity seen from tasseling and six to eight weeks after on silking.
severity_and_yield_loss: Grain yield losses up to 50% or more
Yield losses under artificial epiphytotics estimated up to 66% in susceptible variety Basi and 56.0% in CM 202
Maize yield decreases up to 0.6 t ha-1 when severity reaches more than 75%

cultural_management: Crop rotation of one to two years
Deep burying of infested maize residues before planting maize hybrids
Timely removal of overwintering infected crop residue
Application of adequate potassium in the form of potassium chloride

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Efficacy in controlling TLB both in vitro and in field conditions
Improved seed emergence and seedling vigor and reduced initial inoculum
Improved seed emergence and seedling vigor and reduced initial inoculum
Reduced initial inoculum and disease severity

integrated_management: Seed treatment with carboxin + thiram or benomyl + thiram followed by foliar application of mancozeb (0.25%) thrice at 10 days interval
Seed treatment with carboxin (2 g/kg) and Trichoderma harzianum (6 g/kg) followed by three sprays of mancozeb (0.25%)/propiconazole (0.1%) at 30, 40, and 50 days after sowing

general: Numerous lesions with size up to 2.5 cm long present mostly on the leaves
advanced_symptoms: Later elongate, further becoming rectangular-shaped by restriction of the veins
Color is cinnamon-buff with a reddish-brown margin and occasionally zonate coalescing and becoming grayish with conidia

field_identification: Rectangular-shaped spots with cinnamon-buff color and reddish-brown margins

causes_and_risk_factors: Advance generation hybrids and unmaintained composites
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential to cause grain yield losses of more than 40%
Accounts for 20% or sometimes even more yield losses to maize crop in Pakistan

cultural_management: Early planting in May or June, or late planting in August reduces disease incidence
Manage plant density (minimum incidence at 40,000 ha-1)
Balanced application of phosphorus and potassium reduces disease incidence
biological_management: Inoculation of non-pathogens (Drechslera oryzae and Helminthosporium sativum) on sterilized soil followed by pathogen inoculation

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Completely inhibited growth and conidial germination
Completely inhibited growth and conidial germination
Resulted in the lowest disease index in field experiments

chemical_management.timing: First appearance of disease followed by 2 applications at 10 days interval

general: Appears at a pre-flowering stage in 40-50 days old plants
Starts from the leaf sheath or on leaves in contact with soil and travels up to the ear
early_symptoms: Initially water-soaked and narrow purple-brown bands oriented perpendicular to long axis of leaves or leaf sheath

field_identification: Alternate bleached zones with narrow purple-brown bands perpendicular to the long axis

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Rainfall over 100 mm in the first two weeks of infection

disease_development_and_spread: Secondary spread is due to contact of healthy plants with infected leaves/sheaths.
severity_and_yield_loss: Grain yield reduction up to 31.9% to 90%
Magnitude of grain loss may reach as high as 100% if the ear rot phase predominates

cultural_management: Selection of a well-drained field and planting on raised beds
Composting of hardwood on infested soil
Stripping of the second and third leaf-sheath from the ground level at the age of 35-40 days old crop
biological_management: Trichoderma spp., Gliocladium virens, and Pseudomonas fluorescens

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Good control against banded leaf and sheath blight pathogen
Highly effective seed dressing fungicide with 48.7% disease control and highest yield of 64.7 q/ha over control
Very effective against R. solani and potent to give high level of disease control

integrated_management: Foliar application of carbendazim followed by Trichoderma sprays in sawdust and FYM amended field
Validamycin (0.25%) and T. viride as foliar spray

research_findings: Identified 11 QTLs for resistance to BLSB on chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 10.

general: Small light brownish circular or ovoid spots not more than 4 mm in diameter, surrounded by brown ring

field_identification: Small light brownish circular or ovoid spots (<4 mm diameter) with a brown ring

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed-borne inocula and secondary spread through airborne inocula
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss in maize to the tune of 21-23% in India, and 20-60% in China

chemical_management.timing: Two applications (1st as preventive, 2nd just after appearance of disease)

research_findings: Resistance to CLS was inherited quantitatively and associated with additive and dominant genetic effects accounting for 70% of total phenotypic variation.

general: Minute, round to elongated uredia occurring on both leaf surfaces, husk, and other floral parts
early_symptoms: Pustules are yellowish in the early stage
advanced_symptoms: Pustules become brown and surrounded by chlorotic haloes
visual_field_symptoms: Yellowish to brown pustules on leaves and husk

field_identification: Minute, round to elongated yellowish to brown pustules with chlorotic haloes

severity_and_yield_loss: Losses in grain yields ranging from 6.0 to 36%

general: Chlorotic stunted and yellow to whitish striped leaves giving a 'half disease leaf' appearance
Plants are more erect and slender under congenial conditions
visual_field_symptoms: Yellow to whitish striped leaves with half disease leaf appearance

field_identification: Chlorotic, stunted plants with yellow to whitish striped leaves ('half disease leaf')

severity_and_yield_loss: 81.5% reduction in grain of maize under conditions favoring infection

cultural_management: Sowing with the onset of monsoon or pre-monsoon rains

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Complete protection against Rajasthan downy mildew

general: Infected plants are chlorotic with chlorotic area including the base of the blade with transverse margin
Leaves tend to be narrower and more erect than healthy plants
A white downy mildew growth may appear on lower surfaces of infected leaves
Tassels may exhibit phyllody with no seed set
visual_field_symptoms: Chlorotic leaves with transverse margins, white downy growth underneath, and tassel phyllody

field_identification: Chlorotic leaves with defined transverse margins and white downy fungal growth on lower surfaces

causes_and_risk_factors: Plants less than one-month-old are highly susceptible
disease_development_and_spread: Polycyclic disease cycle capable of causing secondary infections throughout the growing season. Oospores overwinter in soil and plant debris.
severity_and_yield_loss: Severe losses worldwide (in tune of $25 billion)

cultural_management: Removal, destruction, and burning of infected plant debris along with weeds
Rouging of infected plants in early stages
biological_management: Chytrid fungus (Gaeumannomyces spp.) added to soil to parasitize oospores (reduced systemic infection up to 58%)

research_findings: More than 5000 germplasm lines evaluated for host plant resistance.

general: Occurs after flowering stage and prior to physiological maturity
Internal decay and discoloration of stalk tissues
Rotting extends from infected roots to the stalk causing premature drying, stalk breakage, and ear dropping
advanced_symptoms: Affected plants die prematurely producing lightweight ears with poorly filled kernels
visual_field_symptoms: Premature drying, lodging, stalk breakage, and dropped ears

field_identification: Stalk internal decay/discoloration, premature drying, and lodging during grain filling

causes_and_risk_factors: Water stress after flowering / high soil temperature
Excess nitrogen fertilizers compared to potash

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy soil, moisture stress after flowering

disease_development_and_spread: Soil-borne infection pathway; fungus survives on crop residue in soil or on soil surface.
severity_and_yield_loss: Incidence varying from 5 to 40% at different parts of the country

cultural_management: Application of farmyard manure and neem cake
biological_management: Seed treatment with T. harzianum (4 g/kg seed) along with soil application of castor or neem cake (250 kg/ha) 15 days prior to sowing

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: Effectively reduced ear rot disease and fumonisins accumulation

integrated_management: Application of farmyard manure and neem cake along with Trichoderma harzianum 15–20 days before sowing with two additional irrigation at tasseling and silking stage
Integration of T. viride (drenching) with bavistin seed treatment

warnings_and_limitations: Fungicidal control of Fusarium stalk rot is not effective due to its soil-borne infection pathway.
research_findings: Identified QTLs and major genes for resistance on chromosomes 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10.

paper_level_notes: The review provides a comprehensive checklist and distribution of maize diseases in India, including tabular summaries of yield losses, distribution, inoculation techniques, and rating scales.
